title: Beginner To Master | Chess Speedrun | King's Gambit | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We open the King's Gambit — a romantic opening as old as European chess itself, dating to the 16th century.
We play f4, offering the gambit pawn.

A word on f4: it isn't an intuitive move — it actually weakens White's own king, and it took real daring for the old masters to play it. Importantly, the King's Gambit has never been refuted: Black isn't winning and holds no large advantage. But Black does have several ways to reach a comfortable game and defuse White's attack, which is why the opening gradually fell out of fashion.
Declining with ...d6 is passive; more critically Black takes on f4, and White answers with d4.
Black holds the extra pawn with ...g5 — otherwise the gambit makes no sense — and here h4 is the main line, the bishop to c4 a rarer try.

After h4 ...g4, the flashy knight to g5 is interesting but probably unsound — the real move is the knight back to g1: you've softened f4 enough that undeveloping is justified. And against ...g4 the thematic idea is to sacrifice the knight and castle — a Muzio Gambit in spirit, sound because of White's huge lead in development and Black's exposed king.
